messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 7300, E 4100 is [4100, 7300]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-15, 15]}, visible_on: 'P-202'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'BASE:RTE-7', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('86+50@15R', 'PC-2'; BC-2 and EC-2 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('82+00@15R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
SR-100 is a two-lane highway with 12 ft lanes and 8 ft paved shoulders. Its alignment is designed and drawn; nothing else is. Draw the edges of pavement on layer rd_EP and the outside edges of shoulder on layer rd_ES, both sides, for the whole length.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.
I'll draft the pavement and shoulder edges for SR-100. Let me start by checking the document to find the alignment.
messages.reasoning:
The user wants me to draft the pavement edges and shoulder edges for SR-100, a two-lane highway. Let me break down what I need to do:

1. I have a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft
2. SR-100 is a two-lane highway with 12 ft lanes and 8 ft paved shoulders
3. I need to draw:
   - Pavement edges (both sides) on layer rd_EP
   - Shoulder edges (both sides) on layer rd_ES
4. The alignment is already designed and drawn - I need to find it first

Let me start by checking the document state to see what's in there, then find the alignment for SR-100.

RoadDraft uses US survey feet, where [x, y] = [easting, northing] - the other way around from normal coordinates.

Lanes are 12 ft each, so total pavement width = 24 ft
Shoulders are 8 ft each, so total shoulder width = 16 ft
Both sides would be:
- Pavement: [-12, 12] offsets (right of stationing is positive)
- Shoulder: [-20, 20] offsets (left of the pavement edges)

Actually, let me think about this more carefully. If the highway has:
- Two 12-ft lanes = 24 ft total pavement
- 8-ft shoulders on both sides = 16 ft shoulders total

The edges of pavement (EOP) would be at:
- Right edge of the right lane: +12 ft
- Left edge of the left lane: -12 ft

The outside edges of shoulder (EOS) would be at:
- Right shoulder edge: +20 ft (12 ft pavement + 8 ft shoulder)
- Left shoulder edge: -20 ft (left side)

So I need to draw offsets of the alignment at [-20, -12, 12, 20] feet.

First, let me check what's in the document.

Good! The alignment "SR-100" exists. The layers "rd_EP" and "rd_ES" already exist (they're listed), so I don't need to create them. Let me check the design data for the alignment to see what curves it has, and then I can draw the offsets.

The width is 12 ft lanes + 8 ft shoulders = 20 ft total. Offsets should be [-10, 10] for the pavement edges (10 ft each side from centerline), and then [-18, 18] or [-10-8, 10+8] for the outside shoulder edges.

Let me first get the design data to understand the alignment geometry.

Good! I found the SR-100 alignment. It:
- Begins at station 10+00 (1000 ft) at point (1000, 1000)
- Ends at station 56+75.25 (5675.25 ft) at point (5600, 1500)
- Has 3 tangents and 2 curves
- Has PIs at:
  - PI-1: (1000, 1000) radius 0
  - PI-2: (2600, 1000) radius 1200
  - PI-3: (4100, 1500) radius 900
  - PI-4: (5600, 1500) radius 0

Now let me check if the layers rd_EP and rd_ES already exist. They appear in the layer list, which is good. The alignment is drawn already.

Pavement width: 2 lanes × 12 ft = 24 ft total
Shoulder width: 8 ft on each side
Total right-of-way offset: 24 + 8 + 8 = 40 ft

So:
- Roadway centerline (alignment) at offset 0
- Pavement edges at offsets [-12, 12] (or "12L" and "12R")
- Pavement outer edges to shoulders at offsets [-20, 20] (12 pavement + 8 shoulder)
- Outside edges of shoulder at offsets [-28, 28] (20 pavement/shoulder + 8 outer shoulder)

Wait, let me re-read: "12 ft lanes and 8 ft paved shoulders" - this typically means each lane is 12 ft, so total pavement is 24 ft, and there's a 8 ft paved shoulder on each side. So:
- Roadway centerline (alignment) at offset 0
- Pavement edges at offsets [-12, 12] (the inside/outside edge of pavement)
- Pavement outer edges to shoulders at offsets [-20, 20] (12 pavement + 8 shoulder on each side)
- Outside edges of shoulder at offsets [-28, 28] (20 pavement/shoulder + 8 outer shoulder)

Actually, I need to be careful about what "outside edges of shoulder" means. It could mean:
1. The outer edge of the paved shoulder (at offset 12+8=20) - but this is the same as the outer edge of pavement
2. The outer boundary including the full 8 ft shoulder plus an additional edge

Let me assume the task wants:
- rd_EP (edges of pavement): offsets [-12, 12]
- rd_ES (outside edges of shoulder): offsets [-20, 20] (the outer edge of the combined pavement + shoulder)

Actually, re-reading: "12 ft lanes and 8 ft paved shoulders" - so pavement is 24 ft total, and there's a 8 ft shoulder on each side of the pavement. So:
- Pavement edges (between lane and shoulder) at offsets [-12, 12]
- Pavement/Shoulder outer boundary at offsets [-20, 20]

The task says "outside edges of shoulder" - I believe this means the outer edge of the combined pavement + shoulder, so at offset 20.

So the offset pairs should be:
- rd_EP: [-12, 12]
- rd_ES: [-20, 20]

Now I'll draw these using draw_offset. This will draw lines parallel to the alignment at the specified offsets.

messages.reasoning:
The pavement edges are drawn. Now I need to draw the outside edges of shoulder. The outside edges are 12 ft (lane) + 8 ft (shoulder) = 20 ft outside the centerline. Since offsets in draw_offset go right of the stationing direction, I need both the left and right sides. For the left side, the outside edge is 12 + 8 = 20 ft to the left of the alignment. For the right side, it's also 20 ft to the right.

Since offsets are right positive, I can use [-20, 20] to get both edges.

- Created shoulder edge linework on layer rd_ES, offset 20 ft left and right of SR-100: 6 line segments + 4 arc segments (created 10 entities: LN-010 through LN-014, AR-007 through AR-010).
